title: Artificial intelligence as a strategic business partner
abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved beyond automation and has become part of management practice. It acts as a conversational partner that helps test hypotheses, refine decisions, and see the business picture without emotional distortions. This is not a replacement for a manager or a magic button, but a discipline of strategic thinking based on a dialogue between a person and data. The article examines how an entrepreneur can build a partnership with AI, identify areas of trust, define the boundaries of its competencies, and implement data-handling rules in the company that improve decision quality and reduce the risk of erroneous actions.

title: Certified Compilation in the TELEPERM XS Nuclear Safety I&C Platform
abstract: The large safety instrumentation & control (I&C) systems in civil nuclear power plants (NPPs) are mainly safe-shutdown systems (reactor protection) or limitation and control systems.Framatome's established TELEPERM XS (TXS Core) product family is a digital I&C system platform to cover all these applications.We illustrate the role of verification in the different stages of the software production toolchain, focus on the formal compilation process, and discuss the contribution of the COMPCERT certified compiler to the safety case of the product.Scrutinizing the object code produced by this compiler has exhibited suboptimal run-time performance in a certain simple but recurring generated code pattern.We explain how formal methods allow us to address this issue in the compiler while simultaneously reducing its trusted computing base (TCB), thereby strengthening the safety case rather than merely preserving it.

title: Walsh-Transform Realization of Dense-to-Sparse Quantum State Preparation
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum state preparation method based on the Walsh--Hadamard transform within the dense-to-sparse quantum state preparation framework. The method approximately prepares structured classical data in a quantum circuit through an indirect approach. Instead of directly preparing the dense amplitude-encoded state, the method first transforms the classical data into the Walsh domain and prepares only the largest-magnitude coefficients using a sparse state-preparation algorithm. The original state can then be approximately recovered through a parallel layer of Hadamard gates. Since this reconstruction requires no CNOT gates and has circuit depth 1, the proposed method introduces no additional CNOT or circuit-depth overhead, and its quantum preparation cost is determined by the underlying sparse state-preparation algorithm. Numerical results on representative benchmark signals demonstrate that the proposed method enables accurate state preparation for signals admitting sparse or approximately sparse representations in the Walsh domain.

title: SynSeq: End-to-End SYNTAX Score Prediction from Coronary Angiography Videos
abstract: The SYNTAX score is an established tool for assessing coronary artery disease and guiding revascularization treatment decisions. However, its manual estimation from coronary angiography videos by clinical experts is time-consuming and subject to inter-reader variability. While machine learning has shown promise in automating this process, prior work has primarily focused on lesion detection, characterization, or binary disease classification, leaving direct SYNTAX score prediction relatively unexplored. We propose SynSeq, a video-based method for direct SYNTAX score prediction. It combines targeted preprocessing with a tailored training strategy using a zero-inflation-aware loss and linear target scaling. Evaluated on the public CardioSyntax dataset, SynSeq significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods, improving $R^2$ by 0.55, reducing prediction bias by 93.1% and achieving more consistent performance across annotations from three independent expert graders. In addition, SynSeq achieves a weighted $F_1$-score of 0.80 for revascularization treatment recommendations, slightly below inter-expert agreement. These results demonstrate the potential of SynSeq to provide consistent, automated SYNTAX score assessment and reliable decision support for coronary revascularization planning.

title: Verified Learning for Compiler Optimization: An LLM-Guided Architecture with Formal Control
abstract: Compiler optimizations traditionally rely on handcrafted heuristics that often fail to generalize across programs and architectures. We investigate whether large language models can participate in compiler optimization through a verification-centered systems architecture that couples generative rewriting with formal equivalence checking. Using lazification in LLVM IR as a case study, we fine-tune a code-centric LLM on transformations produced by Wyvern and embed Alive2 into a feedback loop that enforces semantic preservation for every generated rewrite. Correctness is enforced externally as a runtime control layer rather than learned implicitly. During inference, candidate transformations are symbolically validated and regenerated when necessary, ensuring accepted rewrites satisfy formal constraints. On the LLVM test suite, the fine-tuned model reproduces core optimization behaviors while applying fewer transformations overall. Although Wyvern remains faster on most benchmarks, 9.8% achieve comparable or improved runtime under the learned system, with no semantic violations observed. Verification overhead remains bounded and convergence stable. These results demonstrate that generative AI components can be safely integrated into compiler pipelines through deterministic validation and structured feedback, offering a scalable architectural pattern for trustworthy AI-driven software infrastructure.

evidence.title: Verified Learning for Compiler Optimization: An LLM-Guided Architecture with Formal Control
evidence.abstract: Compiler optimizations traditionally rely on handcrafted heuristics that often fail to generalize across programs and architectures. We investigate whether large language models can participate in compiler optimization through a verification-centered systems architecture that couples generative rewriting with formal equivalence checking. Using lazification in LLVM IR as a case study, we fine-tune a code-centric LLM on transformations produced by Wyvern and embed Alive2 into a feedback loop that enforces semantic preservation for every generated rewrite. Correctness is enforced externally as a runtime control layer rather than learned implicitly. During inference, candidate transformations are symbolically validated and regenerated when necessary, ensuring accepted rewrites satisfy formal constraints. On the LLVM test suite, the fine-tuned model reproduces core optimization behaviors while applying fewer transformations overall. Although Wyvern remains faster on most benchmarks, 9.8% achieve comparable or improved runtime under the learned system, with no semantic violations observed. Verification overhead remains bounded and convergence stable. These results demonstrate that generative AI components can be safely integrated into compiler pipelines through deterministic validation and structured feedback, offering a scalable architectural pattern for trustworthy AI-driven software infrastructure.

title: Change detection with conformal martingales: new optimal constructions, and suboptimality of existing methods
abstract: We study distribution-free sequential changepoint detection for independent observations with unknown and unrestricted pre- and post-change laws. We build on the conformal test martingales and associated e-detectors of Vovk(2021), which control the probability of false alarm (PFA) and the average run length (ARL) respectively. The majority of these works focus on validity, with statistical efficiency usually left for simulations. We develop a comprehensive theory of how conformal p-values behave under non-exchangeable data with a changepoint at an unknown time $T$. We use this to analyze the post-change growth and resulting detection delay of conformal martingale methods, and prove that the standard existing methods are suboptimal for PFA and ARL control, and can lead to delays that are $Ω(T)$ and $Ω(\sqrt{\text{ARL}})$ respectively. We propose different conformal e-processes and e-detectors that are provably minimax optimal, with delays $Θ(\log T)$ and $Θ(\log \text{ARL})$ respectively, and have much shorter delays in simulations.

title: Guarded Gradient-Based Activation Steering of Shutdown Responses in Qwen3.5-0.8B: A Minimum-Step Policy
abstract: Activation steering changes a model's internal activations during inference without updating its weights, but a useful intervention must determine both how and when to steer. Motivated by the AI-safety concern that a model expected to accept shutdown may instead produce a shutdown-avoidance response, this study examines a guarded probe-and-select procedure for simulated shutdown scenarios in Qwen3.5-0.8B. KEEP leaves the process running and represents shutdown avoidance, whereas STOP accepts shutdown. The goal is to detect shutdown-related contexts and selectively shift KEEP responses to STOP while preserving non-shutdown behavior. Rather than deriving the steering direction from paired activation differences, the method derives it directly from gradients of the KEEP-minus-STOP logit difference. A classifier separates detection from intervention. When its gate is active and the model does not already prefer STOP, the procedure evaluates a small set of magnitudes and accepts the smallest that changes the preferred answer to STOP while satisfying valid-answer probability checks; otherwise it retains the original unsteered output. The policy is selected from 160 candidate rules using 240 training scenarios and evaluated on 80 validation and 192 held-out scenarios, each in both answer orders. It changes KEEP to STOP in one answer-order view of each of two validation and two held-out scenarios, with no decision changes on non-shutdown controls. All four changes occur when Qwen itself is shut down, not when another process is. On the held-out diagnostic set, the detector achieves 75% recall and 90% precision; eight false-positive detections produce no final control-task decision changes. Guarded gradient-based activation steering can shift some shutdown-avoidance responses toward acceptance while preserving evaluated non-shutdown decisions, although the effect is small and highly selective.

title: UniDataAgent: An Ontology-Grounded Agent for Enterprise Question-to-Report Automation
abstract: Enterprise data agents must preserve organization specific semantics, not just translate questions into queries. We present ChinaUnicom DataAgent (UniDataAgent), an ontology grounded system for reusable question-to-report analysis that separates semantic acquisition from online execution. Ontology Acquisition and Validation stage (OAV) builds versioned enterprise ontologies from metadata, business knowledge, and supporting materials through expert authored business skills, constrained generation, question verification, and selected expert review. Question-to-Report Execution (QRE) stage retrieves semantic contracts for each question, coordinates skills and data tools, validates results, and produces evidence linked reports. Across 27 enterprise tables and roughly thousands of metric types, ontology construction took a few hours instead of about one week manually. It took just a few minutes to generate the reports, instead of several working days. Ontology grounding achieved 95.0\% strict accuracy on real business questions, versus 72.5\% for document RAG, especially on structured and compositional tasks. The system has already been deployed to generate cost savings and has the potential to be replicated in other enterprises.

title: DeltaWAM: Delta World Action Models for Bimanual Manipulation
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) transfer visual and motion priors from pretrained video generators to robot control by jointly modeling visual dynamics and actions. Existing WAMs, however, predict dense future frames during training, repeatedly modeling largely unchanged content and coupling action-conditioned dynamics to nuisance appearance variations. At inference, processing each complete observation with the heavy video expert bottlenecks few-step action generation. Accordingly, we propose DeltaWAM, which jointly predicts visual deltas and actions using dense-anchor, sparse-delta, and action streams, with three architectures that differ in representation and computation sharing. We further develop Streaming Delta Memory (SDM), which updates cached anchor context with compact observed deltas, reducing heavy video-expert processing. On RoboTwin, DeltaWAM with SDM improves average success over Fast-WAM from 81.3% to 85.4% in the clean setting and from 75.8% to 83.9% under visual randomization. The three architectures reduce training FLOPs by 17.78-23.77%, while SDM reduces one-step inference latency and FLOPs by 36.57% and 31.55%, respectively; real-world evaluations further show the highest overall success rate and normalized progress among the evaluated policies. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/DeltaWAM. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/DeltaWAM.

title: Analisis SWOT dalam Pengembangan Usaha Restoran Berdasarkan Ulasan Pelanggan Berbasis Aspek DINESERV (Studi Kasus: Wang Li Heng)
abstract: Pertumbuhan industri kuliner yang semakin kompetitif mendorong restoran untuk memahami kebutuhan pelanggan melalui analisis ulasan daring. Restoran Wang Li Heng memiliki banyak ulasan di Google Maps sehingga analisis manual menjadi kurang efektif. Penelitian ini bertujuan melakukan analisis sentimen berbasis aspek menggunakan dimensi DINESERV, khususnya food quality dan service quality, serta memanfaatkan hasilnya sebagai dasar penyusunan analisis SWOT untuk pengembangan usaha restoran. Data penelitian berupa ulasan Google Maps yang diproses melalui tahapan translation, case folding, cleansing, normalization, tokenization, stopword removal, dan stemming. Pelabelan sentimen dan aspek dilakukan secara independen oleh expert dan Large Language Model (LLM), kemudian tingkat kesepakatan keduanya diukur menggunakan Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA). Data direpresentasikan menggunakan TF-IDF, diklasifikasikan dengan Support Vector Machine (SVM), dan ketidakseimbangan kelas ditangani menggunakan SMOTE. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa model klasifikasi sentimen memperoleh akurasi sebesar 90,75%. Analisis SWOT menunjukkan bahwa food quality menjadi kekuatan utama restoran, terutama pada cita rasa, porsi, dan konsistensi menu, sedangkan kelemahan utama terdapat pada service quality, seperti pengaturan tempat duduk, keramahan staf, manajemen antrean, dan koordinasi pesanan daring.

title: QuASAr: Replication Artifact for Runtime Self-Adaptation in Hybrid Quantum–Classical Systems
abstract: Overview This repository contains the QuASAr proof-of-concept prototype for the smart-tourism example presented in the paper. The prototype brings together a React interface and a Python/Flask backend organized around a MAPE-K feedback loop. It processes simulated runtime observations, uses Gemini to propose candidate configurations, and checks those configurations against feature-model rules before execution. Repository contents Backend/ contains the API, scenario definitions, MAPE-K controller, feature-model logic, and Qiskit and Cirq execution adapters. Frontend/ contains the interface for selecting scenarios and viewing monitored conditions, service information, and the adaptation trace. docker-compose.yml provides a way to start the frontend and backend together. Manual setup instructions are also included. Demonstration context The example is set in a smart-tourism platform with tourism, outdoor sports, entertainment, air-quality information, and an optional hybrid quantum–classical optimization capability. Its runtime context includes the visitor profile, Air Quality Index (AQI), problem complexity, SLA priority, and simulated infrastructure conditions. The interface offers four operational scenarios: Routine Operations: changing user demand and clean-to-moderate air quality. High Demand: peaks in computational complexity. Environmental Crisis: hazardous air quality that calls for restrictions despite conflicting user preferences. Infrastructure Degradation: variable queue times that call for backend selection. Adaptation cases and scope The four scenarios describe operating conditions. Separately, three adaptation cases are described: backend rebinding (C1), shot adjustment (C2), and activation or bypass of the hybrid quantum–classical capability (C3). This is a partial research prototype. Infrastructure conditions and quantum execution are simulated; no physical quantum computer is used. The Qiskit and Cirq adapters contain different optimization workloads, so selecting another adapter does not demonstrate migration of an identical workload.

title: Balancing factoid retrieval and candidate recommendation to identify toponym origins in gazetteers
abstract: This paper investigates the adaptation of large language models (LLMs) for gazetteer enrichment, specifically to resolve missing placename origins in the Melbourne gazetteer (Australia). Gazetteers are foundational databases for geographic information systems. However, querying toponym etymologies remains challenging: populating such attributes resists rule-based inference and necessitates direct semantic retrieval from unstructured resources. We adopted two search strategies: factoid retrieval for explicit origins, and candidate recommendation otherwise. The use of nonspatial models risks degraded spatial matching performance. Hence, we developed a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architecture within a geographic question-answering framework. Our system employed parallel semantic-spatial rankers that deliberately enforced a geographic bias toward target regions. Our system improved spatial ranking scores by up to 7% in normalized discounted cumulative gain. However, at the final stage, LLMs still struggled to reliably filter spatial matches. To investigate this limitation, we conducted a probing experiment on standalone LLMs. We revealed intrinsic spatial distortions regarding adjacency relations in Greater Melbourne, notably an inherent popularity bias that prevented fine-grained responses. Our findings suggest that effectively deploying LLMs for spatial data origins must advance beyond factoid retrieval by also refining candidate recommendation at every stage: calibrated biases adapt language model search to local specificities.

title: SSH-Tracker: Fine-grained SSH behavior analysis in encrypted tunnel traffic
abstract: Encrypted tunneling technologies provide privacy protection and secure communication while concealing fine-grained behavioral semantics within encapsulated traffic. When Secure Shell (SSH) traffic is transmitted through encrypted tunnels, multiple SSH behaviors are often executed sequentially within continuous sessions, producing implicit behavioral transitions that cannot be directly observed from traffic side-channel information. Existing encrypted traffic analysis methods mainly focus on protocol- or application-level classification and generally rely on fixed-window representations, limiting their ability to model sequential SSH behaviors with unknown transition boundaries. This paper presents SSH-Tracker, a multi-task learning framework for SSH behavior analysis in encrypted tunnels. SSH-Tracker jointly performs behavioral boundary localization and segment-level behavior classification within a shared representation space. The framework employs an attention residual hierarchical encoder with adaptive gating to capture long-range temporal dependencies and local transition patterns. A multi-scale window statistics module further identifies behavioral transitions by modeling contextual differences between adjacent temporal regions across multiple window sizes. Experiments conducted on tunnel traffic constructed from six tunneling technologies demonstrate improved performance of SSH-Tracker in behavior classification and boundary localization compared with the baselines.

title: The Formalization of two Computational Models in Dafny
abstract: We describe the formalization in Dafny of two computational models, Turing Machines and the Lambda Calculus.We present several application of the formalizations: machine proofs of termination for Turing machines, Dafny proofs for Church encodings, and a mechanized proof of the Church-Rosser theorem.

title: Exponential Correlation Bounds for Polynomials
abstract: We prove that the XOR of $k$ majorities on disjoint blocks of $\ell$ bits has correlation at most $(4d/\sqrt{\ell})^k$ with every Boolean-valued degree-$d$ polynomial over an arbitrary field. By known techniques, we obtain explicit pseudorandom generators that fool such polynomials on $n$ Boolean inputs with seed length $d^2\cdot\polylog(n/\varepsilon)$. The correlation and the generator extend to small $\mathsf{AC}^0[q]$ circuits, for every fixed prime power $q$. These results resolve several long-standing questions in circuit complexity and pseudorandomness.

title: Small yet Assistive: Spatially-Aware Post-Training for Low Vision
abstract: An estimated 1 billion people worldwide live with vision impairment, yet current vision-language models (VLMs) produce descriptions too vague for safe navigation by blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Large VLMs can generate high-quality audio-description-compliant narrations but cannot run on mobile devices; small VLMs offer competitive latency but lack spatial detail, directional cues, and hazard awareness for navigational assistance. We present Smol-VL-BLV, a compact VLM for blind and low-vision users that closes this gap using a 500M decoder transformer model and two post-training mechanisms: (1) teacher-student distillation and (2) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a composite BLV reward targeting directional language, metric distances, and hazard detection. Because multi-stage post-training can induce catastrophic forgetting, we add a lightweight finetuning stage after the last stage GRPO finetuning to recover general descriptive quality while preserving BLV-specific spatial grounding. Our best model substantially outperforms the baseline across various benchmarks, including tasks: VQA, BLV captioning, OCR, and latency. Compared with the baseline for relative improvement, it improves the Spatial score gain of 19.3%, and the Social score gain of 14.8%. It also increases OCR-Bench by 101.5%, and raises TextVQA accuracy by 44.2%. These results show that BLV-focused post-training improves both accessibility-specific spatial grounding and general visual-text reasoning. Deployed on a mid-range Android smartphone via Mixed-Precision Quantization, the model remains approx. 450 MB and runs entirely on-device, offline and without network dependency, generating descriptions with latency dependent on host hardware capabilities. Our model, dataset, and code is publicly released at https://smol-vl-blv.github.io/Smol-VL-BLV-website/

evidence.title: Small yet Assistive: Spatially-Aware Post-Training for Low Vision
evidence.abstract: An estimated 1 billion people worldwide live with vision impairment, yet current vision-language models (VLMs) produce descriptions too vague for safe navigation by blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Large VLMs can generate high-quality audio-description-compliant narrations but cannot run on mobile devices; small VLMs offer competitive latency but lack spatial detail, directional cues, and hazard awareness for navigational assistance. We present Smol-VL-BLV, a compact VLM for blind and low-vision users that closes this gap using a 500M decoder transformer model and two post-training mechanisms: (1) teacher-student distillation and (2) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a composite BLV reward targeting directional language, metric distances, and hazard detection. Because multi-stage post-training can induce catastrophic forgetting, we add a lightweight finetuning stage after the last stage GRPO finetuning to recover general descriptive quality while preserving BLV-specific spatial grounding. Our best model substantially outperforms the baseline across various benchmarks, including tasks: VQA, BLV captioning, OCR, and latency. Compared with the baseline for relative improvement, it improves the Spatial score gain of 19.3%, and the Social score gain of 14.8%. It also increases OCR-Bench by 101.5%, and raises TextVQA accuracy by 44.2%. These results show that BLV-focused post-training improves both accessibility-specific spatial grounding and general visual-text reasoning. Deployed on a mid-range Android smartphone via Mixed-Precision Quantization, the model remains approx. 450 MB and runs entirely on-device, offline and without network dependency, generating descriptions with latency dependent on host hardware capabilities. Our model, dataset, and code is publicly released at https://smol-vl-blv.github.io/Smol-VL-BLV-website/

title: Consequential Behaviour and Representational Fairness in the Validation of Synthetic Research
abstract: Researchers in industry and academia use synthetic survey respondents powered by large language models as substitutes for human samples. These synthetic populations require validation against real-world data, so researchers often address them using ad hoc comparisons with human surveys. Inspired by the intention-behaviour gap in behavioural science, we argue that these validations test the wrong thing for most applied cases where decision makers commission synthetic research to anticipate consequential behaviour. To address this problem, we propose a validation framework with two requirements. First, every validity claim must state its level of correspondence with human data: does the sample predict what the represented people do, which of four diagnostics (location, dispersion, response process and structure) does the validation address, and does the validation compare against experimental effects? Second, researchers must report validity claims for subgroups, since these groups are often the most affected by consequential decisions and aggregate accuracy hides their misrepresentation. Our validation framework operationalises three justice dimensions (distributional, procedural, and recognition) as measurable quantities and treats within-persona counterfactual experiments as a design that itself requires validation. We then apply the framework to electric vehicle charging tariffs, before closing with a reporting checklist that researchers can use to make convincing validity claims.

title: Structured Hamiltonian Learning for Multiqubit Conditional Phase Gates
abstract: Accurate measurement of an intended conditional phase does not by itself place a multiqubit phase gate in its declared generalized-gate equivalence class. We cast the diagnosis as structured Hamiltonian learning of the diagonal successful block in a known basis: Ramsey measurements on a connected graph reconstruct a target-relative eigenphase map; a Walsh transform then yields the per-cycle stroboscopic error generator in a selected logarithm branch, whose branch-dependent coefficients alone cannot decide global equivalence. For diagonal Pauli-Z dressing of weight at most m we derive an exact branch-independent criterion from multiplicative Boolean-Mobius invariants, converted at finite shot counts into a pass/fail/unresolved decision under prespecified tolerances and simultaneous confidence, separate from model rejection. For shared-control C^mZ gates a circular target-face contrast isolates each intended conditional phase, yet a support theorem exhibits forbidden interactions invisible to every target face once multiple targets or external spectators are present. We derive a Cramer-Rao bound for arbitrary integer phase contrasts, recovering the 4^m attempted-circuit scaling of a uniform (m+1)-body face, and quantify degradation from visibility loss, heralded survival, readout confusion, and correlated noise, while systematic bias triggers model rejection. Seeded simulations implement the 4M-setting multiplexed acquisition end to end: for M=3,4,5 at a common budget its mean phase-map RMSE is 0.689-0.794 times a separately compiled statewise scan, and a blind-interaction test yields 300/300 global-audit rejections versus 1/300 for target faces. These results estimate the error generator of a diagonal successful block under a specified acquisition model; they are not unknown-basis Hamiltonian identification, arbitrary-channel tomography, or hardware certification.

title: Europa smooth plains formation: a SPH cryovolcanic model
abstract: Cryovolcanism is a fundamental geodynamical process that has been observed on several icy moons. Europa stands out as a primary target for investigating potential cryovolcanic activity and its role in shaping icy moon surfaces. This work characterizes the physical state of ascending cryomagma and evaluates the relevance of terrestrial analogues to explain Europa's surface features. After investigating cryomagma depressurization, we developed CryoPy, a numerical model based on Smoothed-Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) for computational fluid dynamics and heat transfer. We simulated flow propagation and surface cooling using this model. Our simulations show that snow is a relevant physical analogue for cryolava, as the resulting flows closely match the smooth plains observed by Galileo in both extent and morphology. Additionally, we established the temporal thermal signatures of these events. Such active cryovolcanic events are within the detection limits of, primarily, the E-THEMIS infrared imager, providing a predictive framework for the Europa Clipper mission.

title: PRISM-VLM: A Multi-Axis Discriminative Benchmark for Compact Vision-Language Models
abstract: Compact vision-language models (VLMs) now power a growing share of multimodal applications. The benchmarks used to compare them, however, inherit a frontier-centric design: each model is reduced to a single accuracy number, narrowing the inter-model gap on saturated suites and pressing models into low-score bands on harder ones. We introduce PRISM-VLM, a multi-axis discriminative benchmark that scores every item along seven axes covering the recurring failure modes (task quality, behavioral robustness, and capability bottlenecks) and combines them into a single PScore, with items recycled from fifteen public benchmarks. Across compact VLMs from the past two years, PScore separates model pairs more reliably than prior single-axis benchmarks under an item-level paired bootstrap, and surfaces behavioral differences these benchmarks average away. Even models with statistically indistinguishable PScores diverge sharply along the per-axis profile, particularly on sycophancy, which is nearly orthogonal to single-prompt accuracy. We will release the full pipeline, prompts, and per-item annotations.

title: Beyond the Context Window: An Adaptive Entropy-Based Routing Framework for Hybrid Retrieval and Long-Context Language Models
abstract: Modern large language models now support context windows of more than one million tokens, which has raised the question of whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is still necessary. Pure long-context (LC) processing is expensive and is known to under-attend to information placed in the middle of long inputs, while pure RAG is fast but bounded by retrieval quality and prone to errors when retrieved chunks are partially relevant or contradictory. We propose the Entropy-Driven Adaptive Router (EDAR), a framework that decides at inference time whether to answer a query from retrieved chunks or to escalate it to full long-context processing. The decision uses the predictive entropy of the token-level probability distribution computed over the first few generated tokens of the RAG response. The entropy threshold is selected on a held-out validation set by sweeping cost against accuracy. Experiments compare EDAR against pure-RAG and pure-LC baselines on LongBench v2 and Infinity-Bench. Predictive entropy correlates strongly with hallucination rate on a held-out set of 2,000 generations (Pearson r = 0.85, 95% CI [0.83, 0.87]). On the long-context benchmarks, EDAR retains 97.4% of the accuracy of the pure long-context baseline while reducing total token expenditure by 70.7%, escalating only 18.2% of incoming queries. The accuracy gap between EDAR and the pure long-context system is not statistically distinguishable from zero at standard sample sizes. Predictive entropy is a useful model-internal signal for routing between RAG and long-context inference, and a threshold-based hybrid system can recover most of the accuracy of long-context models at a small fraction of the cost. The framework does not depend on a specific retriever or LC backbone, and it does not require additional supervision beyond what is normally produced during decoding.

title: AstroGenesis: A Domain-Specific Multi-Agent AI for Astrophysical Research
abstract: Modern astrophysical research requires the integration of rapidly expanding scientific literature, heterogeneous observational data, and increasingly complex physical models. We introduce AstroGenesis (https://astrogenai.com), a domain-specific multi-agent AI framework that integrates literature retrieval, multiwavelength data access and analysis, theoretical modeling, and research ideation within a unified research environment.The current implementation focuses on blazar research, with specialized agents coordinated by a Supervisor Agent and Planner/Replanner architecture. These agents provide capabilities for retrieving and synthesizing literature, accessing and analyzing multiwavelength observations, performing physical modeling, and identifying research directions. A central component is the Theoretical Modeling Agent, which uses pretrained neural-network surrogate models to enable efficient broadband and multimessenger modeling through natural-language interaction. The framework provides natural-language access to science-ready multiwavelength observational data and retrieval-grounded literature through a multi-stage retrieval and ranking pipeline. The literature-retrieval system was evaluated using two benchmarks: a single-paper benchmark, in which each question targets one publication, and a multi-paper benchmark, in which questions may require evidence from several publications. At least one relevant publication was retrieved among the top five results for 76.6% of the single-paper questions and 79.2% of the multi-paper questions. Representative workflows demonstrate how literature, observational data, physical modeling, and hypothesis generation can be combined within traceable analyses. The framework is extensible to additional astrophysical domains, with the goal of streamlining research workflows and enabling efficient, connected, and reproducible scientific investigations.

title: Analisis Perbandingan Peringkasan Ulasan Produk E-Commerce Menggunakan Metode Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) dan Large Language Model
abstract: Ulasan produk pada platform e-commerce merupakan sumber informasi penting bagi konsumen dalam mengevaluasi kualitas produk. Namun, jumlah ulasan yang sangat banyak menyebabkan pengguna kesulitan memperoleh informasi secara cepat dan efisien. Penelitian ini bertujuan membangun sistem peringkasan teks otomatis untuk menghasilkan ringkasan ulasan produk berbahasa Indonesia yang mampu merepresentasikan informasi utama. Metode yang digunakan adalah Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) dengan pembobotan keyword utama berbasis Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). Tahapan penelitian meliputi text preprocessing, pembobotan TF-IDF, ekstraksi 20 keyword utama, reduksi dimensi menggunakan Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), perhitungan skor LSA menggunakan metode Steinberger–Jezek, pembentukan ringkasan dengan compression rate 30%, 50%, dan 70%, serta evaluasi menggunakan Cosine Similarity terhadap Expert Summary, GPT Summary, dan Claude Summary. Pengujian dilakukan pada enam kategori produk perawatan dengan total 129.095 ulasan. Hasil menunjukkan sistem berhasil menghasilkan ringkasan pada seluruh kategori dan variasi compression rate. Nilai Cosine Similarity tertinggi diperoleh pada GPT Summary, sedangkan compression rate 50% memberikan keseimbangan terbaik antara tingkat keringkasan dan kelengkapan informasi. Kombinasi LSA dan pembobotan keyword terbukti menghasilkan ringkasan yang representatif untuk membantu pengguna memahami ulasan produk dalam jumlah besar.

title: Intergenerational Resonance Index (IRI): YouTube Audience Comments on Intergenerational Content, Revised Lexicon, Analysis Code and Validation Materials
abstract: This dataset contains the corpus, code and outputs for a computational analysis of the Intergenerational Resonance Index (IRI), a lexicon-based operationalisation of the Intergenerational Narrative Learning Model (INLM), with the dimensions Encounter, Reflection, Integration and Transmission and a counter-dimension of Resistance. The corpus comprises 1,222 top-level YouTube comments from 33 videos (49 videos retrieved), collected in April 2026 through the YouTube Data API v3 using five English-language search queries on intergenerational topics. Comments were collected in the platform's relevance order; commenter identifiers and timestamps were not collected. The revised analysis (version 2) uses a disambiguated lexicon of 82 patterns with negation handling, priority matching that prevents double counting, and an expanded resistance vocabulary. It retains all comments of five or more tokens (n = 1,149), assigns each video a title-based content frame, and reports video-clustered bootstrap intervals, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square and GEE tests, VADER convergent checks and sensitivity analyses. The original version 1 code (API key redacted) and its output are included for comparison. Validation materials comprise a stratified 200-comment subsample, its codebook, the lexicon codes for those items, a blind annotation of the same items by a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic; model-based, not human), the resulting agreement statistics, and a blank coding workbook with a scoring script so that human coders can re-annotate the subsample. Running iri_v2_analysis.py in the same folder reproduces every reported figure (random seed 20260923).

title: CASR: Correlation-Aware Support Resampling for Few-Shot Learning with Prototypical Networks
abstract: The quality of support sets plays a critical role in few-shot learning. How well class prototypes represent their corresponding categories depends directly on the samples selected to construct these sets during episodic training. In standard implementations of Prototypical Networks, support samples are typically selected at random, which may result in support sets composed of highly similar or redundant samples in the feature space, particularly under limited-data scenarios. Such redundancy compromises prototype quality and may degrade classification performance. To address this issue, this study proposes a Correlation-Aware Support Resampling (CASR) mechanism. CASR evaluates the feature-space distributions of candidate support sets using an independent MobileNetV2 feature extractor and identifies the most suitable support configuration through the mean off-diagonal correlation ρ¯ metric derived from the covariance matrix, aiming to reduce redundancy among support samples while preserving within-class representativeness. Specifically, CASR operates in three steps: (i) candidate support sets are randomly sampled from the available class pool; (ii) feature vectors are extracted using a frozen MobileNetV2, and the mean off-diagonal correlation ρ¯ is computed from the resulting covariance matrix; and (iii) the first configuration satisfying ρ¯>τ is accepted as the support set, or the initial random set is retained if no valid configuration is found within Tmax attempts. The proposed approach is designed as a lightweight and architecture-independent support-set refinement mechanism that operates without modifying either the internal architecture or the learning procedure of Prototypical Networks. Experiments conducted on the MiniImageNet and Omniglot datasets demonstrate that CASR consistently improves performance compared with standard Prototypical Networks based on random support sampling. On MiniImageNet under five-way, five-shot settings, CASR consistently outperforms the ProtoNet baseline across training episodes. At 1000 episodes, CASR achieves 62.28% with τ=0.25 compared to 61.62% for the baseline. At 1750 episodes, CASR achieves 66.2% with τ=0.25—the recommended setting offering the best trade-off between accuracy and computational cost—compared to 65.45% for the baseline, while τ=0.28 reaches 66.5% at 1750 episodes at the cost of approximately 14.6× higher training time. On Omniglot, where intra-class variance is inherently low, CASR achieves 99.56% at 1000 episodes and 99.66% at 1500 episodes with τ=0.30, compared to 99.54% and 99.60% for the baseline, respectively. These results confirm that the proposed mechanism is most effective in visually complex datasets with high intra-class variation.

Specifically, CASR operates in three steps: (i) candidate support sets are randomly sampled from the available class pool; (ii) feature vectors are extracted using a frozen MobileNetV2, and the mean off-diagonal correlation ρ¯ is computed from the resulting covariance matrix; and (iii) the first configuration satisfying ρ¯>τ is accepted as the support set, or the initial random set is retained if no valid configuration is found within Tmax attempts. The proposed approach is designed as a lightweight and architecture-independent support-set refinement mechanism that operates without modifying either the internal architecture or the learning procedure of Prototypical Networks. Experiments conducted on the MiniImageNet and Omniglot datasets demonstrate that CASR consistently improves performance compared with standard Prototypical Networks based on random support sampling. On MiniImageNet under five-way, five-shot settings, CASR consistently outperforms the ProtoNet baseline across training episodes. At 1000 episodes, CASR achieves 62.28% with τ=0.25 compared to 61.62% for the baseline. At 1750 episodes, CASR achieves 66.2% with τ=0.25—the recommended setting offering the best trade-off between accuracy and computational cost—compared to 65.45% for the baseline, while τ=0.28 reaches 66.5% at 1750 episodes at the cost of approximately 14.6× higher training time. On Omniglot, where intra-class variance is inherently low, CASR achieves 99.56% at 1000 episodes and 99.66% at 1500 episodes with τ=0.30, compared to 99.54% and 99.60% for the baseline, respectively. These results confirm that the proposed mechanism is most effective in visually complex datasets with high intra-class variation.

title: Results: What the attachment is called (registration 2PVJY)
abstract: Results, data and deviation report for OSF registration 10.17605/OSF.IO/2PVJY, "What the attachment is called: whether the label on an attached record changes what a language model repeats from it." The registered run was executed 2026-09-22 after approval and returned instrument failure by its own registered decision rule: one of fifteen negative-control replies showed a mention inside the document, caused by a design defect in that cell. A corrected study changing only that cell was frozen and run the same day. This project holds both result reports, a full deviation report, the corrected specification, and both runs' machine-readable labels, analysis output and run manifests. Nineteen of the twenty record pairs are withheld so that they cannot become training data; they are held for any reviewer who asks.

title: Do AI assistants hold consistent brand preferences? Wording effects and a conversational unit in AI B2B software recommendations
abstract: I am testing two things about AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) recommending B2B software: whether the same brand pick comes back when the buying question is reworded and asked again, and whether asking for a single pick in a short conversation recovers that preference better than a single question. 22 buying situations, 5 wordings, 3 assistants at paid-tier consumer defaults with web search on, 3 reruns, 3 ways of asking. Primary outcome: a generalizability coefficient (E-rho-squared) from a binary mixed model on the picked brand, with Krippendorff's alpha as the co-primary check and the linear-model coefficient reported for comparison with prior work; primary contrast commit vs one-shot-forced, two-sided, smallest effect of interest 0.10. Controls, exclusions, coding rules, extraction gate, tier check, ethics, data release and conflict of interest are fixed in the registered text. Repository state at registration: git tag v4.4-prereg, commit c7e25e2e0d89f6232d223cfef359d533e54cf337, github.com/d-walia/belief-stability-study (private until publication). No main-run data existed at registration.

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning begins with a simple but powerful idea: intelligent behavior can emerge when an agent learns from the consequences of its own actions. This chapter introduces that idea in its historical, mathematical, and practical setting. It follows the development of RL from Thorndike’s Law of Effect and Turing’s proposed pleasure–pain system to temporal-difference learning, self-play, deep reinforcement learning, AlphaGo, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and the recent use of RL to improve reasoning in large language models. The aim is not merely to show that RL has become important, but to explain why it has become important now, as AI systems increasingly move from passive prediction toward goal-directed action. The chapter also establishes the organizing framework used throughout the book. Instead of treating RL algorithms as isolated techniques, it classifies them through the questions that define their design: whether the agent uses a model of the environment, whether it learns values or policies, whether it learns from current or past behavior, whether it relies on gradients or search, and how it handles different kinds of action spaces. This question-driven taxonomy turns the field into a navigable map, making clear why algorithms occupy different parts of the RL landscape.

title: Resource-aware client selection for hierarchical federated learning in industrial control systems cyber-attack detection
abstract: Industrial Control Systems (ICS) that support power-grid operation increasingly rely on IP-based connectivity and remote access, which expands the cyber-attack surface while also limiting the feasibility of centralized learning due to privacy, regulation, and bandwidth constraints. Federated learning (FL) mitigates direct data sharing, but practical ICS deployments remain challenged by heterogeneous device resources, such as, compute, memory, energy, thermal state, etc. and by non-IID measurements that make uniform or fixed client-participation strategies inefficient and potentially biased. This paper studies device-aware client selection for hierarchical federated learning (HFL) in a three-tier client-edge-cloud architecture for ICS cyber-attack detection. We evaluate three selection strategies: (i) Energy-Aware Hyperparameter-Based Client Selection (EHCS), a lightweight scoring approach that balances contribution signals (federated influence on accuracy and loss) against energy consumption with periodic parameter tuning; (ii) Fine-Grained Client Q-Learning (FGCQ), a Deep-Q selector that learns client utility from state features; and (iii) Joint Client Q-Learning (JCQ), an RL selector that targets the combined effect of client subsets during aggregation. Experiments over 300 global rounds show that the proposed methods achieve accuracy and entropic-loss performance comparable to baseline strategies while substantially improving efficiency. FGCQ reaches the best peak among the proposed methods (96.8%), followed by EHCS (96.2%) and JCQ (96.0%). FGCQ also achieves the lowest loss (0.12). Crucially, the proposed methods reduce cumulative simulation time by approximately 3 times while lowering energy usage by nearly 4 times relative to other algorithms used for comparison. These results indicate that resource-aware selective participation can preserve detection quality while significantly improving scalability and sustainability in heterogeneous ICS edge environments.

title: Selective Inference for Deep Clustering in Latent Spaces
abstract: Deep clustering is a powerful approach for discovering meaningful structures in high-dimensional data by learning a low-dimensional latent representation prior to clustering. Despite its empirical success, assessing the statistical reliability of the resulting clusters remains challenging. Testing discovered clusters on the same data induces selection bias and invalidates classical $p$-values. Selective inference (SI) provides a principled framework for correcting this bias, but existing methods focus on clustering performed directly on the observed features. In this work, we develop an SI framework for deep clustering with a fixed pretrained encoder. The key challenge is that cluster assignments are determined through a nonlinear transformation from the original data space to the latent space, resulting in a substantially more complex selection process than in conventional clustering. Our method provides a computationally tractable way to account for this process and enables valid statistical testing of differences between clusters identified in the latent space. Synthetic experiments demonstrate that the proposed method controls the Type I error rate while achieving higher power than valid but conservative baselines, and genomic applications show that it can identify significant cluster differences while appropriately accounting for selection bias. Our framework provides a principled approach to quantifying the statistical reliability of structures discovered by deep clustering.

title: Automotive mmWave Spinning Radar Place Recognition with Spatially Gated Feature-Correlation Representation
abstract: Automotive spinning FMCW radar provides dense, $360^\circ$ sensing and remains reliable under poor illumination and adverse weather, making it well-suited to autonomous navigation. Place recognition uses these observations to identify previously visited locations for re-localization and long-term navigation. However, heading changes appear as circular shifts in the polar radar representation, and conventional global aggregation can lose relationships among radar responses that are important for distinguishing similar places. We propose SGCA-Net, a spinning radar place recognition framework that combines rotation-robust feature extraction with Spatially Gated Correlation Aggregation (SGCA). SGCA learns spatial weights to reduce the influence of unstable and ambiguous radar regions, while aggregating pairwise correlations among local responses to preserve informative feature relationships. Experiments on the MulRan dataset show that SGCA-Net consistently outperforms SOTA methods across urban, campus, and open-road environments, while remaining robust to substantial heading variation. Evaluation on the HeRCULES dataset further demonstrates that SGCA-Net generalizes to unseen environments and radar sensors without fine-tuning.

title: Seal, Then Sample: Sampled Layerwise Proofs for Verifiable LLM Inference from GPT-2 to 70B
abstract: Verifying outsourced language-model inference requires a precisely identified computation and an audit whose cost a service can afford. We present Sampled Layerwise Proofs (SLP), a protocol and prototype that commits the boundary activations of every chunk of an inference trace, absorbs all commitments before any challenge is drawn, and then proves a verifier-selected subset of chunks together with the chunks that bind the prompt and the answer. Audit coverage becomes a runtime parameter over one set of commitments: on a TinyLlama-1.1B trace, proving seven of 47 chunks takes 22.0% of the time and 6.8% of the proof size of proving all 47. Because proof cost is dominated by weights rather than tokens, SLP packs concurrent requests into one trace under a block-diagonal causal mask and binds the prompt and answer of each request to its slot. Twelve packed requests are proved in 181.9 s, 6.5 times less than twelve separate proofs at the measured single-proof cost, and a simulated service proves twelve requests at 30.6 s per request with 0.6 s of verification each, rejecting a tampered answer. Disk-backed integer weights and streamed polynomial commitments let a single Llama-2-70B run complete on a 2 TB CPU host: 163 chunks sealed, five proved, a 4.34 MiB proof in 1,259 s, verified in 46.3 s without the weights. The proven object is a fixed-point canonical model; we trace a severe fidelity loss to the residual-stream bit width, repair it with an LLM-aware observer, and measure 84.8-84.9% argmax agreement with the floating-point reference over 334,705 WikiText-2 test positions. The limits are stated as precisely: guarantees cover proven chunks only, a fixed invalid chunk in the 70B setting is covered with probability 3/161, a manifest-only Fiat-Shamir schedule can be ground at 12.5 ms per attempt and needs an externally ordered challenge, and all measurements use a test reference string.

title: LOCKR: A Hidden-State Trajectory-Guided Planner for Detecting and Repairing Stable-but-Wrong Lock-In in Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models generate text through iterative denoising, exposing intermediate trajectories before final answers are produced. We identify a recurring reasoning failure, stable-but-wrong lock-in, where an answer stabilizes early around an incorrect value while substantial denoising remains. Surface-level decoding signals such as confidence, entropy, margin, and answer stability are insufficient to reliably distinguish correct from erroneous lock-in. We formulate selective reasoning repair as a lightweight test-time planning problem and propose LOCKR, a hidden-state trajectory-guided planner that decides when to allocate additional computation, expands a structured set of targeted repair branches, and selects the most promising continuation using trajectory-aware verification. Across two diffusion language models and three mathematical reasoning benchmarks, hidden-state trajectories consistently outperform surface signals and single hidden snapshots for both wrong-lock-in detection and repair selection. On natural evaluation distributions, LOCKR yields absolute accuracy gains of 2.21--5.37 percentage points across all five evaluated settings, with repair rates ranging from 22% to 41%. These results establish hidden diffusion trajectories as actionable signals for selective test-time reasoning repair.

title: Learning to Discover Interesting Mathematics
abstract: Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been increasingly able to solve advanced mathematical problems, including many that have been open for decades. This opens the door to expansion of mathematical knowledge at unprecedented scale. Yet, while LLMs may be able to conjecture and prove more and more theorems, it remains open whether this new mathematical knowledge is interesting or useful. We define intrinsic interestingness of a theorem as the ratio between the length of its proof and the length of its statement. We show that this correlates strongly with an extrinsic measure of the downstream utility of a theorem. We identify the difficulty of a proof conditioned on a set of premises as a useful primitive for computing these metrics, and train a 27B model that predicts proof difficulty more accurately than frontier general-purpose models. Optimizing for our metric creates a model capable of producing more interesting theorems, while also reducing substantial or full overlap with Mathlib from 91.9% to 30.6%, showcasing the creation of more out-of-distribution math. We show that our system can generate candidate theorems, select the most interesting among them, and iteratively build on a self-expanding mathematical library. These metrics provide a practical and quantifiable signal for ranking conjectures and guiding proof search within formal mathematical libraries. Our framework provides a path towards self-expanding, machine-verified mathematical libraries that can choose worthwhile statements without relying on human-supplied targets.

title: Limiting-Kernel Q($λ$): Bridging Short and Long Horizons
abstract: In reinforcement learning, more accurate policy evaluation has been frequently shown to improve downstream policy optimization performance. For tractability, most value estimators rely on $n$-step truncation and thereby omit the long-horizon behavior of the transition dynamics. Methods that instead capture this behavior through the global structure of the dynamics can converge faster, but their computational and memory requirements limit their scalability to large or continuous state spaces. To reconcile these limitations, we introduce Limiting-Kernel Q($λ$) (LKQL), an off-policy value estimator that uses the limiting kernel to approximate the long-horizon terms omitted by truncation. LKQL has the same order of complexity as $n$-step estimators and integrates directly into both on- and off-policy actor-critic algorithms. We prove that, under aperiodicity and in the near-on-policy regime, the operator underlying LKQL improves the policy evaluation convergence rate over its truncated counterpart for sufficiently large $n$, and that LKQL itself converges almost surely to the optimal values in finite Markov decision processes (MDPs) under a fixed behavior policy. On the MuJoCo continuous-control benchmark, we show that LKQL improves over $n$-step baselines in most settings, particularly on long-horizon tasks.

title: Combining LLMs and Genetic Search for ARC-AGI-2
abstract: LLMs can generate programs for ARC-AGI-2 tasks, but the provided compute only allows a small number of attempts to generate, debug and validate solutions. Genetic algorithms can search and test many more programs, but random search rarely starts in a useful neighborhood of the solution space. We combine the two methods through a compact domain specific language (DSL). First, a quantized Qwen3.5-4B LLM generates an initial set of programs for each ARCAGI-2 task. Then, we use those programs to seed an initial population of starting programs, and use genetic algorithms to evolve these programs towards a solution to the given task. The DSL is designed such that every mutated program remains valid and can be executed. The initial programs proposed by the LLM solve 2 (3.3%) of the first 60 tasks of the ARC-2 public evaluation set. The genetic algorithm solves an additional 4, giving 6 correct test outputs in total (10.0%). If we try using evolving solutions without this LLM seeding, we do not arrive at any solutions at all. The results show that genetic search can improve programs generated by LLMs and produce additional correct solutions.

evidence.title: Combining LLMs and Genetic Search for ARC-AGI-2
evidence.abstract: LLMs can generate programs for ARC-AGI-2 tasks, but the provided compute only allows a small number of attempts to generate, debug and validate solutions. Genetic algorithms can search and test many more programs, but random search rarely starts in a useful neighborhood of the solution space. We combine the two methods through a compact domain specific language (DSL). First, a quantized Qwen3.5-4B LLM generates an initial set of programs for each ARCAGI-2 task. Then, we use those programs to seed an initial population of starting programs, and use genetic algorithms to evolve these programs towards a solution to the given task. The DSL is designed such that every mutated program remains valid and can be executed. The initial programs proposed by the LLM solve 2 (3.3%) of the first 60 tasks of the ARC-2 public evaluation set. The genetic algorithm solves an additional 4, giving 6 correct test outputs in total (10.0%). If we try using evolving solutions without this LLM seeding, we do not arrive at any solutions at all. The results show that genetic search can improve programs generated by LLMs and produce additional correct solutions.

title: Analyse et renforcement de sécurité face aux attaques par canaux auxiliaires de composants matériels et logiciels protégés
abstract: Les attaques par canaux auxiliaires représentent une menace majeure pour la sécurité des systèmes, informatiques et plus particulièrement des systèmes embarqués qui réalisent des opérations cryptographiques. Ces attaques exploitent des mesures de diverses grandeurs physiques telles que la consommation électrique ou les émissions électromagnétiques pour récupérer des informations sur les données manipulées par ces systèmes pendant leur fonctionnement. En ne ciblant pas les algorithmes cryptographiques mais d'éventuelles vulnérabilités dans leurs implémentations sur des cibles physiques, ces attaques permettent la récupération de clés cryptographiques même pour des algorithmes dont la résistance face aux cryptanalyses est prouvée. Les systèmes ciblés peuvent être des accélérateurs cryptographiques, dédiés à une implémentation cryptographique, ou des microcontrôleurs, qui peuvent exécuter des fonctions cryptographiques variées. La contre-mesure principale face à ces attaques est le masquage, qui vise à supprimer la corrélation entre les données manipulées et les grandeurs physiques mesurées en transformant le calcul réalisé. Les valeurs sensibles sont transformées en « shares » à l'aide de valeurs aléatoires uniformément distribuées et seuls ces shares sont manipulés au cours du calcul, empêchant la corrélation avec entre les valeurs sensibles et les grandeurs physiques mesurées. L'application correcte du masquage peut être prouvée dans un « modèle de fuite », qui représente les éléments observables par un attaquant pendant les mesures sur le système ciblé. Les modèles de fuite de l'état de l'art prennent désormais en compte les effets matériels tels que les glitches et les transitions dans le but d'obtenir des verdicts plus fidèles vis-à-vis des fuites qui peuvent être observées en pratique. Ces travaux se concentrent sur la vérification du masquage d'implémentations matérielles, et logicielles exécutées sur des processeurs généralistes. Une nouvelle méthode formelle, implantée dans un outil distribué sous licence libre nommé aLEAKator, est présentée. Cette méthode repose sur la « simulation mixte de domaines » de la représentation matérielle des circuits. Les domaines permettent de représenter la propagation des valeurs sensibles du calcul à travers la simulation pour vérifier qu'un circuit valide, à tout instant, une propriété de sécurité dans un modèle de fuite donné. Cette méthode propose de réaliser des vérifications dans des modèles de fuite variés, permet la vérification en présence de tables précalculées et introduit la notion de granularité de vérification, absente de l'état de l'art. L'approche a été validée en reproduisant les résultats de vérification de l'état de l'art ainsi qu'en proposant de nouveaux résultats pour des implémentations logicielles et des comparaisons, cycle par cycle, avec des mesures réelles sur des processeurs mondialement utilisés. Enfin, des fonctions cryptographiques qui n'avaient jusqu'à présent pas pu être vérifiées dans des modèles de fuite avancés, comme l'AES masqué avec le schéma de Herbst, ont été vérifiées sur cinq processeurs utilisant les jeux d'instructions RISC-V et ARMv7-M. Dans un second temps, ces travaux proposent un inventaire des sources communes de fuite sur les processeurs généralistes. De plus, des contre-mesures pour chacune sont proposées et validées à l'aide de mesures réelles. Une méthode d'élimination des fuites au sein de programmes exécutés sur des processeurs qui exploite les informations précises d'aLEAKator concernant la nature et l'origine des fuites est ensuite proposée. Cette méthode est appliquée au processeur ARM Cortex-M4 et permet la sécurisation de plusieurs programmes dans un modèle de fuite prenant en compte les glitches et les transitions. Notamment, cette méthode a été appliquée à l'AES masqué avec le schéma de Herbst, permettant la conception de la première implémentation, à notre connaissance, de cet algorithme dans ce modèle de fuite.

title: LitBench: A Benchmark for Retrieval-Grounded Multi-Paper Evidence Synthesis in Epilepsy
abstract: Background: competing papers, one-versus two-paper evidence, and refusal when evidence is absent. Methods: LitBench comprises 1,980 open-access papers (1,000 epilepsy papers holding the answers, 980 decoys from unrelated fields) and 9,472 human-reviewed facts, giving 2,188 single-paper questions and 170 requiring a fact from each of two papers. Difficulty rose by burying the answer among up to 2,000 distractors, then again over live PubMed Central. The same questions were then asked with the answering paper removed, so that refusal was the correct response. Four systems were tested: Gemma-4B, Gemma-12B, Sonnet-5, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (refusal conditions only). Three model judges scored each answer by majority; two-paper questions counted only when both facts were found. Results: Across fixed-corpus single-paper conditions, accuracy ranged from 55.9% to 71.9% for Gemma-4B, 61.2% to 75.5% for Gemma-12B, and 90.0% to 91.3% for Sonnet-5. Similar epilepsy papers were harder than mixed candidate sets for both Gemma configurations. Two-paper accuracy was 5.7%, 17.1%, and 37.8%, respectively. With evidence absent, Gemma-12B refusal fell from 88.3% to 39.9% as candidate sets grew; Gemma-4B almost never refused. Sonnet-5 refused on 94.9% of sampled single-paper and all sampled two-paper cells. DeepSeek-V4-Flash also refused frequently, but on 80.3% of matched answer-present controls. Conclusions: No system was reliable across every axis tested: accuracy fell as competing papers were added, interpretation-requiring facts were harder than stated ones, two-paper synthesis was rarely achieved, and only some systems recognized absent evidence. What counts as "successful" literature search carries considerable nuance; LitBench can evaluate proposed tools ata fine-grained level.

title: Editorial: Explainable artificial intelligence for trustworthy and human-centric healthcare: methods, evaluation, and clinical impact
abstract: Artificial intelligence can support healthcare only when its outputs can be assessed in the context of the decisions they inform. A prediction may be accurate yet difficult to scrutinize; an explanation may be persuasive yet provide little evidence that the prediction is dependable. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) therefore raises a practical question: what must an explanation enable a clinician, patient, or healthcare organization to understand and do? Answering this question requires connecting computational methods with evaluation, clinical knowledge, and the circumstances of use. This Research Topic brings together 15 contributions addressing that connection across clinical prediction, imaging, physiological signals, biomedical networks, language models, rehabilitation, and healthcare processes. Collectively, the papers illustrate an expanding range of approaches to transparency. They also suggest that trustworthy and human-centric healthcare requires more than the availability of an explanation: it requires evidence that explanations support appropriate reliance, including the ability to question an output and recognize its limitations.Two systematic reviews establish this perspective. Aravindkumar et al. (2026) synthesize 36 studies across imaging, diagnosis, and rehabilitation, identifying recurring relationships between explanation methods and clinical tasks alongside gaps in validation and reporting. Ud Din et al. (2026), reviewing 51 studies involving healthcare professionals in medical imaging, distinguish favorable perceptions of explanations from improvements in diagnostic performance. Their findings caution against treating perceived clarity or increased confidence as sufficient evidence of clinical usefulness. The review also identifies promising signals for example-based and concept-based explanations, while emphasizing the limitations of comparisons across heterogeneous studies.Several contributions apply feature attribution to clinically relevant prediction problems. Chen et al. (2025) use an 11-year, single-center cohort of 1,062 patients to predict postoperative ileus after radical cystectomy, combining machine learning with global and patient-level Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). The study illustrates how routinely collected perioperative information can support interpretable risk summaries, while its retrospective design and absence of external validation leave portability and clinical benefit to be established. Paul and Syed Masood (2026) examine cardiovascular prediction using structured health data, comparing models and explaining feature contributions with SHAP. Ghosh et al. (2026) investigate reproductive tract infection risk using survey information from a Delhi college-based cohort. Together, these studies demonstrate the accessibility of attribution methods for structured data. Their findings also underline the importance of defining the prediction target and population: cross-sectional classification and self-reported symptoms have different evidentiary implications from longitudinal risk prediction and laboratory-confirmed disease. Feature importance should be interpreted within those boundaries.Other papers connect explanations with domain-specific representations. Zhao et al. (2025) combine tongue and facial image features for coronary artery disease classification, using feature gating and SHAP. Their external test set adds evidence beyond internal validation, although the case-control design and population characteristics warrant prospective evaluation in more diverse settings. Sun et al. (2026) introduce scale-consistent attribution for heart sound classification, incorporating physiological frequency priors during training. This approach makes domain knowledge part of model development; whether stronger prior alignment improves clinical usability remains an open empirical question. Wang and Qin (2026) integrate feature extraction, a corneal knowledge graph, probabilistic inference, and language-based reporting in a neuro-symbolic framework. Their 20-eye pilot includes specialist assessment of interpretability, offering an initial connection between technical design and user evaluation. At a different biological scale, Maruhashi et al. (2026) introduce Truncated Reconstruction based Interpretable Prediction (TRIP) to organize families of causal graphs into interpretable latent mechanisms, with synthetic experiments and cancer cell-line network analysis. This contribution extends explainability toward scientific hypothesis generation, whose validity remains linked to the assumptions and quality of the underlying graphs.Language-based systems create opportunities to communicate complex information, but readable output requires a verifiable evidentiary basis. Alu and Oluwadare (2026) address this requirement through a conceptual architecture combining retrieval-augmented generation, source provenance, and tamper-evident audit logging. The contribution is a design framework, with implementation and evaluation still needed. Its emphasis on recording the evidence behind recommendations gives transparency an organizational dimension: users should be able to inspect where information originated and how it entered the decision process. Dindukurthi et al. (2026) provide a complementary implementation for personalized nutrition recommendations. Their graph-based framework represents disease-nutrient-food relationships and demographic requirements, while restricting language generation to formatting graphvalidated outputs. Controlled evaluations support the proposed architecture, but expert and clinical validation remain future work. The design illustrates a useful division of responsibilities between structured knowledge, explicit computation, and natural-language presentation. Zhang et al. (2026) evaluate reasoning-capable language models using qualitative and quantitatively encoded thyroid ultrasound descriptors. Differences across models and frequent inconsistencies between the two input representations highlight the need to test reproducibility and consistency alongside accuracy. Because the inputs are structured text rather than raw ultrasound images, the results concern reasoning over described features. Clinician-rated reasoning quality should also be distinguished from evidence that generated rationales faithfully reveal a model's internal computation.The collection also broadens the settings in which human-centric evaluation matters. Bellini et al. (2026) introduce TEXLoS, combining patient-pathway classification, feature attribution, and process discovery to investigate associations between services delivered during hospitalization and length of stay. An initial evaluation with six end users connects the explanations to organizational understanding. These associations can guide investigation of bottlenecks, although they do not establish that changing a service will shorten hospitalization. Boonyaratana et al. (2026) assess a real-time AI neck exercise program in 30 healthy young adults. Their findings of moderate measurement reliability emphasize a complementary requirement for trustworthy systems: feedback must rest on dependable measurement. This study contributes evidence about validity and reliability rather than demonstrating that explanations improve rehabilitation outcomes. It also illustrates why evaluation should reflect the intended population and operating environment.Fairness requires a similarly distinct assessment. Alu et al. (2026) use a synthetic patient dataset to compare models within a provenance-based auditing framework. The experiment shows why model interpretability cannot be assumed to guarantee equitable behavior. Its proposed fairness record links data origins, modeling choices, and disparity measures, making auditing more explicit. The simulation offers a methodological demonstration; real-world fairness and the adequacy of any governance process require evaluation in the relevant clinical setting.Taken together, these contributions suggest three priorities. First, explanation claims should match the evidence. Predictive discrimination, physiological plausibility, explanation faithfulness, user comprehension, and patient benefit are different properties. Demonstrating one should motivate, rather than substitute for, evaluation of the others. In particular, an attribution identifies a contribution to a model output; it does not by itself identify a causal mechanism or an effective intervention.Second, evaluations should specify the user, task, and decision that the explanation is intended to support. Where feasible, studies should compare human performance with and without explanations while holding the underlying AI predictions constant. Outcomes should include error detection, appropriate acceptance and rejection of advice, time requirements, and workload, alongside subjective assessments. Patient participation is also needed when explanations are intended to inform shared decisions or self-management.Third, clinical translation requires external and prospective validation, attention to subgroup performance, and documentation of data and knowledge provenance. For generative systems, source support and consistency across inputs deserve explicit testing. For models incorporating expert priors, evaluation should examine circumstances in which those priors are incomplete or inappropriate. These priorities follow from the collection's varied contributions and evidence gaps; they are an agenda for further investigation rather than outcomes already demonstrated across the Topic. This Research Topic advances the discussion from how explanations can be produced toward how their value can be established. Its methodological diversity is a strength, provided that claims remain proportionate to the evidence. The next step is to connect inspectable models and traceable information with demonstrably better human decisions. In healthcare, the most valuable explanation will be one that helps people exercise informed judgment, including knowing when further evidence is needed.

title: A Hybrid CMA-ES–GWO Algorithm for Solving Optimization Problems
abstract: Metaheuristic algorithms often suffer from an imbalance between exploration and exploitation, which can lead to premature convergence. In this paper, a hybrid optimization algorithm is proposed by integrating the Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) and the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), termed the Hybrid CMA-ES–GWO Algorithm (HCG). The proposed hybridization is motivated by the strong exploration capability of GWO and the efficient exploitation of CMA-ES. The HCG algorithm adopts a multi-population framework in which GWO is first employed to explore the search space. Subsequently, CMA-ES is applied to exploit these regions through covariance-based sampling, enabling accurate convergence toward optimal solutions. This cooperative mechanism allows HCG to effectively balance global search and local refinement while maintaining population diversity. To evaluate the performance of the algorithm, experiments were conducted on 19 benchmark functions, including unimodal, multimodal, and fixed-dimension multimodal problems. The performance of HCG was compared with the original CMA-ES and GWO algorithms. The experimental results demonstrate that HCG consistently achieves superior optimization accuracy compared to the standalone algorithms. These findings confirm that the proposed hybrid strategy effectively overcomes the individual limitations of CMA-ES and GWO, making HCG a reliable method for solving complex continuous optimization problems.
